q2: SELECT alias1.c1, alias2.c1 FROM t5 AS alias1 JOIN t5 AS alias2 ON alias1.c1 <> alias2.c1 WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM t5 AS alias3 LEFT JOIN t5 AS alias4 ON alias3.c1 <> alias4.c1 WHERE alias4.c2 IS NULL);
explanation:
Q1 looks at every pair of rows (b1 , b2) coming from table t1 and compares the *sets* of t5.c2 values that are linked to those two c1-values.  It only returns the pair when the c2-set of b1 is a proper subset of the c2-set of b2 (subset and not equal).

Q2, on the other hand, is almost independent of such set logic.  The correlated NOT-EXISTS block in its WHERE clause is **not correlated at all** – it does not reference alias1/alias2.  That sub-query merely checks whether t5 contains at least two different c1 values.  • If t5 has ≥2 different c1 values, the sub-query is empty, NOT EXISTS is TRUE and Q2 returns **all** pairs of different c1 values occurring in t5.  • If t5 has only one c1 value, Q2 returns nothing.

Hence, whenever t5 holds at least two different c1 values whose c2-sets are identical, Q2 will still output every cross-pair, whereas Q1 will output none (because no strict-subset relationship exists).
counterexample_dsp: Create two distinct c1 values (’A’ and ’B’) in t1.  Give them exactly the same single c2 value (’X’) in t5.  Because the c2-sets of A and B are equal, Q1 finds no strict subset and returns an empty set, whereas Q2 sees two different c1 values in t5, its NOT-EXISTS test succeeds globally, and it outputs the pairs (A,B) and (B,A).

Q1 looks at every pair of bars (t1 rows) and compares the COMPLETE set of beers (t5.c2 values) they sell.  It only outputs (b1 , b2) when the beer set of b1 is a PROPER subset of the beer set of b2 (all beers of b1 are also sold by b2 and b2 sells at least one extra beer).

Q2 uses grouping and joins instead of correlated-subqueries.  It keeps the pair (bar1 , bar2) when
  • bar1 and bar2 sell at least ONE common beer (inner join on t5.c2), and
  • bar2 sells MORE beers in total than bar1 (count2 > count1).
It does NOT demand that every beer of bar1 is also sold by bar2 – only that they share at least one.  Therefore pairs that overlap partially, but where bar2’s total count is larger, are produced by Q2 while being rejected by Q1.

  Set(A) = {x , y}
  Set(B) = {x , z , w}
A and B overlap (x), |B| > |A|, but A is NOT a subset of B (because y∉B).  Q2 keeps (A , B); Q1 rejects it.  No other subset relation is present so Q1 returns no rows.

explanation:
Q1 first finds, for every t2 row, the minimum c3 that appears in t5 (sub-query).  It then LEFT-joins t5 again **on (t2.c1 = t5.c2 AND t5.c3 = that minimum)** and returns t5.c1. explanation:
Q1 first takes the minimum price per product-key t5.c2 (GROUP BY c2). It then keeps only the t5 rows that have exactly that minimum price, and finally LEFT-joins that information to every row of t2. Therefore, for every value of t2.c1 at most the rows whose price equals the global minimum for that c2 survive.
Q2, on the other hand, groups by the pair (c2, c1). Because c1 is part of the primary key of t5, each (c2,c1) group contains at most one row, so Q2 in practice just echoes every row of t5 (with its own price) – one row per (c2,c1).

counterexample_dsp: Have one product key (c2 = 'X') present in t2, and two different sellers (c1 = 'A' and 'B') for that product in t5, with different prices (10.00 vs 5.00).  Q1 will output only the seller with the lowest price (B, 5.00), whereas Q2 will output both sellers (A,10.00) and (B,5.00).  All inserts respect primary- and foreign-key constraints.

q2: SELECT alias1.c1, alias1.min_price, t5.c1 FROM (SELECT t2.c1, MIN(t5.c3) AS min_price FROM t2 LEFT JOIN t5 ON t2.c1 = t5.c2 GROUP BY t2.c1) AS alias1 NATURAL JOIN t5;
explanation:
Q1 looks for the cheapest (MIN c3) t5-row per product id t5.c2 and then LEFT-joins that minimum back to t5 again on (t2.c1 = t5.c2 AND min_price = t5.c3).  Therefore it compares t2.c1 with t5.c2 and keeps every t2 row even when no matching t5 row exists, because both joins are LEFT OUTER.

Q2 first computes the same minimum price per t2.c1, but afterwards it performs a NATURAL (INNER) JOIN with t5.  A NATURAL JOIN matches the columns that share the same name – here that is column c1 – so Q2 compares alias1.c1 (== t2.c1) with t5.c1 and, being an INNER join, discards rows that do not satisfy this equality.

Thus the queries differ as soon as there is a t5 row whose c2 equals a t2.c1 (so it contributes to the minimum price used by Q1) while its c1 is different from that t2.c1 (so Q2’s NATURAL JOIN does not match it).  In that situation Q1 outputs the t2 row (with the minimum price and the foreign t5.c1), whereas Q2 outputs no row at all.
counterexample_dsp: Have one product row in t2 (c1 = 'A').  Put one price row in t5 whose c2 = 'A' (so it belongs to that product) but whose c1 is a different key (e.g. 'X').  Because Q1 compares t2.c1 with t5.c2 it finds the row, while Q2 compares t2.c1 with t5.c1 and finds nothing.  Necessary supporting rows are added to t1 so the foreign-key from t5.c1 is satisfied.

Q1 first computes the minimum price that appears in t5 for every value of t5.c2 (subquery).  It then keeps ONLY those t5-rows whose price equals that minimum, and returns (t1.c1 , that c2 value, min-price).  
Q2 starts from every row of t2, joins to t5 and, for every pair (t2.c1 , t5.c1) produces the minimum price found in that pair; groups that have at least one matching t5 row are kept.  Thus Q2 can return one row per (c2,c1) pair, whereas Q1 returns at most one row per c2 (and only for the rows that realise the global minimum price in that c2).  
As soon as a given t5.c2 (coming from t2.c1) has two different t5.c1 values with different prices, Q2 will output both bars, while Q1 will output only the bar(s) whose price equals the overall minimum.  Therefore the queries are not equivalent.

Q1 will only keep the row whose price is 4.00, while Q2 will output both rows, because it groups by the extra column t5.c1.
